docs.text: Byrgenwerth Bloodborne Paleblood is a decompilation of Bloodborne with its own runtime, one verified function at a time We are born of the blood, made men by the blood, undone by the blood. Our eyes are yet to open… Fear the old blood. Master Willem / The Blood Minister Paleblood is a decompilation of Bloodborne ( PS4 , CUSA03173, version 1.09) with its own runtime : a functional decompilation , the game's code rewritten function by function as readable C++ that does exactly what the original did, and a runtime of our own for that code to run on. The game doesn't run on Paleblood yet: 21 of 157,757 functions are verified (0.01%). On our own runtime the executable's boot gets as far as scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (libkernel, called by libc.elf), with 238 of 686 system imports provided. Runtime status Paleblood is building its own runtime . The project-owned boot harness currently reaches the executable's entry and stops at an unresolved system import. Full game runs still use an external host scaffold while the project-owned runtime is completed. See the Runtime page for the current boot result. 14,010 bytes verified 0.0330% of all game code 21 functions verified 157,757 functions in the game 238 / 686 system imports provided loaded boot milestone (0 of 8) 2026-10-06: 4,711 bytes verified, 9 functions 2026-10-07: 11,933 bytes verified, 20 functions 2026-10-09: 11,933 bytes verified, 20 functions 2026-10-10: 14,010 bytes verified, 21 functions 2026-10-06 — 4,711 B 2026-10-10 — 14,010 B Verified replacement code by day — see the devlog for the story behind each step. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony Interactive Entertainment or FromSoftware in any way. Why we do this Because we love this game. Yharnam deserves to outlive the hardware it was made for, and to be understood as well as it is loved: every function of the original, read, named, rewritten and proved to behave exactly as it did, so that one day it runs natively, at any frame rate, for as long as there are hunters to play it. The goal A complete source port of Bloodborne for the PC. When the hunt is over, every function of the game's 1.09 executable will have been rewritten as readable C++ and proved to behave exactly like the original, and the game will run natively on Paleblood's own runtime : no PS4 , no emulator, no original executable, only the game's data from your own copy. Because it will be source, the game can be read, understood, preserved, fixed and modded like any other program, at any frame rate and resolution. Two tracks get there, side by side: Decompilation: functions rewritten as readable C++ and proved against the original in the verification harness , on inputs recorded earlier and on generated edge cases . Runtime: our own loader (done), generic input capture (foundation in place; integration incomplete), kernel, threads and memory, files, input, audio, video out, and the graphics, rebuilt at the engine's own level rather than by emulating the PS4 's GPU ( Runtime ). The game does not run on Paleblood until the runtime is far enough along that road. A place to learn This wiki is also an educational resource, and that is one of its most important jobs. Every page is written so that someone who has never taken a game apart can follow how it is done, and see why each step is taken, not only what was found. You do not need a console, a dump or any game files to read and learn from it; the project only ever shows how the game's code works, in our own words and our own code. What you can learn here: How a console game is put together : the PS4 executable and its libraries, how the game's frame loop paces itself, how its systems (timing, input, rendering, AI, characters) talk to each other. Start with Architecture and How the Frame Limiter Works . Reverse engineering in practice : reading disassembly, telling what a function does from its callers, callees and the memory it touches, and the traps in the tools ( Ghidra & PS4 Quirks , the system pages ). Proving code correct : how a rewritten function is checked against the original on real and hand-made inputs, and why deliberately wrong versions must fail ( Architecture: Verification ). The words : every term of the trade, explained in the Glossary ; hover a dotted term anywhere for its meaning. The devlog tells the same story as it happened, mistakes included. Key documents Document What it covers Architecture The two tracks, the verification harness , the frame pipeline Runtime Our own runtime : the roadmap and how far the game's executable boots on it How the Frame Limiter Works The first system replaced , step by step Glossary PS4 and project terms explained Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Traps in the tools and the ABI Contributing Joining, the first pull request, the rules Methodology Each function goes through five steps before it is marked verified : Analyze — Ghidra with the GhidraOrbis loader finds the function in your own dump; its callers, callees and the memory it touches are read from the disassembly, not only the decompiler. Name — it gets a name and a system in the shared function table, so every contributor's Ghidra shows the same names. Rewrite — a readable C++ version: named structures instead of raw offsets, named calls instead of addresses, named constants, faithful to what the original does. Verify — the harness runs the original and the replacement on the same inputs, recorded in earlier game runs and generated for the corners, and compares return values, registers, every byte written and every library call. Deliberately wrong versions must fail. Review — an independent reviewer checks the verification and the readability. A function whose code no recording reaches yet is edge-verified until one does. Legal Tools and source only — no game files, no extracted assets, no decompiler dumps. Everything starts from your own console and your own copy: to contribute or verify you need Bloodborne (CUSA03173, EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from your own PS4 . The project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools. How to read it The executable keeps its code in one block from 0x00400000 ; read-only data, the exception tables and the writable data follow it and are not code, so they are not on the map. A slice's address range says nothing about what system lives there: the game's systems are spread across the executable. The system pages say which functions belong where. The bar of a slice with replaced code is drawn at least a little wide so a single small function stays visible. Layout of the executable Range What 0x00400000 … Code ( .text ): every function the map shows after the code Read-only data, .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr (unwind tables) after that Writable data and zero-initialized data The exact block boundaries are the GhidraOrbis loader 's; see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks for how they were checked against the unwind tables.

docs.text: The executable keeps its code in one block from 0x00400000 ; read-only data, the exception tables and the writable data follow it and are not code, so they are not on the map. A slice's address range says nothing about what system lives there: the game's systems are spread across the executable. The system pages say which functions belong where. The bar of a slice with replaced code is drawn at least a little wide so a single small function stays visible.
docs.title: How to read it

docs.text: Range What 0x00400000 … Code ( .text ): every function the map shows after the code Read-only data, .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr (unwind tables) after that Writable data and zero-initialized data The exact block boundaries are the GhidraOrbis loader 's; see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks for how they were checked against the unwind tables.

docs.text: Architecture How Paleblood fits together: two tracks, decompilation and runtime , and how a function moves from original code to verified , readable C++. At a glance Your own pkgs base + 1.09 update prepare_dump.sh extract, merge, SELF to ELF, hash check Ghidra + GhidraOrbis eboot.elf: names and sizes into symbols/ Paleblood's loader map, relocate, bind every import Boot harness the entry on our runtime, to the first gap Verification harness original and replacement, same inputs Runtime libraries kernel, files, input, audio, video, GNM Readable C++ verified and independently reviewed The game runs on Paleblood once the runtime is far enough along Paleblood is a decompilation with its own runtime . The decompilation rewrites the game's code, function by function, as readable C++ that is proved to behave like the original. The runtime is what that code, and the original executable while it is being replaced , runs on: Paleblood's own loader and a growing set of PS4 system-call implementations. The game does not run on Paleblood's runtime yet; the Runtime page has the roadmap, implemented calls, and the latest saved boot result. Full game runs still use an external host scaffold while the project-owned runtime is completed. The verification harness independently maps the executable and replays recorded inputs. Its capture writer now supports stable, function/run-identified output and replay checks, but it has no production call sites yet and does not automatically provide new game inputs. A synthetic host test checks Paleblood's side of the versioned plug-in interface; it does not exercise the external host or establish full-run equivalence. The decompilation track A replacement lives in the code repository's game/<system>/ and is written to its style rules: the objects a function touches described as structures with named fields, the original's other functions and globals reached through named declarations instead of addresses, named constants, and no test plumbing inside the game's code. A function reaches the main branch only when it is both verified and readable, and an independent reviewer, not the author, has checked both. Replacements are registered in a hook table. When the runtime runs the game, each registered function's entry will jump to its replacement, so every caller lands in the new code: a 14-byte jump, which is why a function shorter than that cannot be hooked this way. The runtime track Paleblood's loader maps the game's executable, together with the game's own C library and file system modules, applies every relocation and binds every system import, to one of those modules or to the runtime 's own implementation. The boot harness then runs the executable's entry and stops at the first system function the runtime does not implement yet, naming it. Each step of the runtime 's work implements what the boot stops at, written clean-room from public documentation and our own reverse engineering. The frame pipeline The first system decompiled. Solid boxes are verified C++; dashed boxes are still original code. next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work Once per frame the frame step checks that the window is running, creates the SprjFlipper on the first frame (its constructor reads Game.FlipMode ), lets the flipper's limiter wait out the frame, and runs the game's task update. The full walk-through is in How the Frame Limiter Works . Verification Earlier game runs inputs recorded while the game ran Edge-case generators what a recording does not reach Capture library captures/ / _NNNN.json harness.py our loader; original and replacement, same inputs verify.py compare returns, registers, bytes, calls Mutation test wrong variants must fail edge-verified, verified plus the independent review A replacement is checked against the original outside the game. The harness maps the executable from your own dump with Paleblood's loader , scripts every library call the function makes, runs the original and the replacement on the same inputs, and compares return values, callee-saved registers, every byte written and every library call. The inputs are cases recorded in earlier game runs (the capture library) and edge cases generated for the corners. Deliberately wrong versions of the replacement must fail; if one passes, the cases are too weak and get fixed first. A function whose code no recording reaches yet is edge-verified ; it becomes verified once recordings for it exist and pass, and the independent review has approved it. Addresses Every address in this wiki is a PS4 virtual address with the executable at 0x400000 , the convention of the community patches. See Ghidra & PS4 Quirks . What comes next The queues live in the code repository's NEXT.md : one for the decompilation track, one for the runtime track.

docs.text: CI Setup Both repositories run GitHub Actions on every push and pull request. Neither ever sees game data: nothing from a dump is in the repositories, and CI does not need it. Code repository ( Paleblood ) .github/workflows/ci.yml runs three jobs: a GCC/Clang build matrix, policy, and a pull-request session report. build (gcc) and build (clang) — configure and build with CMake, run the syslib CTest (the RT_SYSLIB unit test) on every push and pull request, then run the remaining CTest suite. It includes hook -table and loader tests, a mock-host test of Paleblood's versioned plug-in interface, boot and tooling checks, and synthetic harness cases. The mock host does not run the external game-run scaffold or establish native game-run equivalence. policy — rejects anything that looks like game data; validates the function tables; checks that runtime and tools name nothing specific to the game; checks that the README progress matches tools/progress.py ; runs the readable-code check (addresses, raw offsets, magic numbers, and recording code); and exercises the pre-commit hooks . session report — on pull requests, CI selects the concise report for runtime -only changes, the documentation report, or the full decompilation/mixed report from changed file paths. Unknown code paths fail closed to the full report. Runtime changes cannot downgrade a mixed PR. The build and policy jobs still apply to every path. Function-level verification against the real game cannot run in CI, because it needs your dump. It remains required for decompilation changes and runs locally ( tools/verify.py run , tools/smoke.sh ). The full session report must include every replacement status change recorded for the PR and matching, non-empty, passing verify.py evidence for each replaced , edge-verified , or verified function. Runtime-only contributions do not require a dump, captures , or function-level verification. After a runtime PR merges, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts its result on the PR. tools/promote.py checks existing recorded and edge cases locally and requires an approved review before promotion. Comparison result files go to temporary storage; the capture library remains input-only. --dry-run leaves verification metadata and function status unchanged. Wiki ( Byrgenwerth ) .github/workflows/ci.yml installs MkDocs, rejects game data, checks that every generated file (progress data, tables, visuals) agrees with the data it comes from and that no page has a hand-typed count, builds the site with --strict , and exercises the pre-commit hooks . Local workflow (no CI needed) Shell tools/install_hooks.sh # both repositories tools/smoke.sh # code repository: the pipeline on a known function export BB_PORT_DIR = /absolute/path/to/clean-paleblood-main-at-merged-sha tools/end_session.sh # wiki: pull numbers from the code repository, build, check python3 -m mkdocs serve # wiki: preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 For wiki validation and publication, pin BB_PORT_DIR to a clean worktree at the exact merged Paleblood revision and record its absolute path and full SHA in the shared checkpoint. Do not use the implicit sibling checkout when it may contain uncommitted or stale changes.

docs.text: Contributing Tonight, Gehrman joins the hunt. Gehrman, the First Hunter Paleblood is open to everyone. This page is the short version; the full rules are in the code repository's CONTRIBUTING.md , and the step-by-step setup in its ONBOARDING.md . Questions go in Discussions . Ways to help Name functions — the good first issues: small functions with a clear purpose, identified from their callers and the library calls they make, named in the shared function table. Document a system — a page here per system: summary, key functions, structures, patch points, open questions. Replace functions — readable C++ replacements, verified against the original with the harness and reviewed independently. Build the runtime — claim a call or tightly related group in its system issue ( #34–#41 ), then use a runtime/<function> branch to implement it in RT_SYSLIB with unit tests. Runtime-only work is clean-room, needs no game dump or captures , and receives maintainer boot verification after merge; see the runtime syscall notes and full workflow in Paleblood's contribution guide. Tooling — the harness , the capture library, the Ghidra scripts. Your own copy Decompilation work starts from your own console and your own copy of the game: Bloodborne (CUSA03173, EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from your own PS4 . Runtime-only contributions do not need a dump, captures , or any game files. The project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools. Requests for game files, or links to them, are removed wherever they are posted, and may lead to a ban. Ground rules No game files. Ever. No executables, assets, decompiler output or extracted data in commits, issues, pull requests or Discussions. No screenshots or clips of the game in the code repositories, their issues, pull requests, Discussions, or documentation site. Verified and readable. A replacement that "looks right" is not done until the harness finds no difference on recorded and edge cases , deliberately wrong versions fail, it reads well (the code repository's STYLE.md), and an independent reviewer has approved it. The local promotion tool reruns the recorded and edge suites before changing a function to verified ; its comparison output is temporary and kept away from the capture library. Case data stays on the contributor's machine. Say how you know. When you name a function, say how you inferred what it does: its callers, its library calls, the memory it touches. A name says what is known and no more. One pull request per function or cluster , with the disclosures CONTRIBUTING.md asks for. Getting started Fork Paleblood on GitHub and run tools/install_hooks.sh in your clone. For decompilation, follow ONBOARDING.md from your own dump to Ghidra . For runtime work, read the syscall notes and claim one function or related group in its system issue (#34–#41); use a branch named runtime/<function> . Keep one function or tightly related group per PR. Add RT_SYSLIB unit cases and include evidence, confirmed behavior, unresolved questions, and test results in the runtime report. Runtime-only PRs run the compiler matrix, RT_SYSLIB tests, and repository policy checks without requiring a dump, captures , or function-level verify.py . After merge, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts the result on the PR.

docs.text: Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Grant us eyes, grant us eyes! Plant eyes on our brains, to cleanse our beastly idiocy! Micolash, Host of the Nightmare Traps in the tools and the PS4 ABI that cost time. This page is the code repository's QUIRKS.md , copied in by tools/sync_progress.py , so the two never disagree. Traps in Ghidra and the PS4 ABI that cost time. Entries marked unconfirmed come from general PS4 / Orbis knowledge and have not been checked on this target yet; confirm or correct them when you hit them. The converted executable The ELF has no section headers (confirmed). The Orbis loader ( GhidraOrbis ) synthesizes blocks from the program headers: the executable PT_LOAD becomes .text , and its own heuristic splits .rodata , .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr off the end of it. The progress denominator is the functions Ghidra finds in that .text block, so it depends on the loader and the analysis. progress.py ties its numbers to the hash of the committed export, and the export prints how many functions fell outside .text . .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr are marked executable by the loader ; they are data. e_type is 0xfe10 (confirmed), not ET_EXEC or ET_DYN . The first PT_LOAD has p_vaddr 0, so the file does not say where the game lives; the convention below does. Ghidra 's default for this file type is unconfirmed : always set the image base explicitly on import and check it (the export script refuses any other base). Program headers include Sony types ( PT_SCE_* , PT_SCE_DYNLIBDATA and friends) that Ghidra does not understand. The PT_INTERP is /libexec/ld-elf.so.1 (confirmed). Dynamic linking data is in a Sony-specific segment, so Ghidra will not resolve imports by itself. SelfUtil-Patched removes the repeated data before the first segment (at 0x4000) and patches the version segment. Another SelfUtil build can produce a different file with different hashes: always check target.sha256 . Address conventions All addresses in this repository are PS4 virtual addresses: the ELF p_vaddr plus 0x400000 , with Ghidra 's image base set to 0x400000 . Community patch files use the same address convention. Three conventions exist, one constant apart. V is the ELF p_vaddr . Convention Address Where it appears ELF virtual address V ELF program headers and file layout PS4 virtual address V + 0x400000 ours , Ghidra , community patch files To convert an address to the ELF virtual address, subtract 0x400000 . tools/validate_functions.py rejects any address below 0x00400000 , which catches a base-0 import by mistake. Checked against the target image (read-only): - The community "Performance Patch" address 0x0261B108 minus 0x400000 holds c7 45 b4 06 00 00 00 ( mov dword [rbp-0x4c], 6 ), which the patch changes to 9. Tool-independent identity: the loaded image (loadable segments copied to their p_vaddr , SHA-256) of this target is 071df19c8880086d97182dbc057bc8cb37badaca57d9112683836b24a0444c0a . It is the same whichever SelfUtil build produced the ELF . Ghidra itself Ghidra 12 headless has no Jython: a .py script fails with " Ghidra was not started with PyGhidra". Our scripts are Java GhidraScripts. support/analyzeHeadless hardcodes MAXMEM=2G . That is too small for this binary; raise it in that file (setup in docs/GHIDRA.md). The Orbis loader replaces an image base of 0 by 0x1000000 by default. Pass -loader-imageBase 0x400000 ( -loader-baseAddr is ignored by this loader ). -loader "Orbis ELF" is rejected by headless as an invalid loader name; leave -loader out, the Orbis loader is picked automatically for this file. Calling convention Orbis uses the System V AMD64 ABI: integer arguments in rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9 , floats in xmm0-xmm7 , return in rax:rdx / xmm0:xmm1 , callee-saved rbx rbp r12-r15 . Variadic callers set al to the number of vector registers. Leaf functions use the 128-byte red zone below rsp . Ghidra 's stack analysis can read that as unused or mis-size the frame. Optimized code splits and merges functions (tail calls, shared epilogues, cold paths in the same range). A "function" boundary in Ghidra may be wrong. Check the call sites before you claim a size. Parameters Ghidra types as undefined8 are often pointers or floats in another register class. Read the call sites, not the decompiler's signature. Ghidra can pick a wrong calling convention for functions that pass a struct or this in an unusual register. Fix the signature before trusting the output. CPU The CPU is an AMD Jaguar: SSE up to 4.2, AVX and F16C, BMI1. No AVX2, BMI2 or FMA3 ( unconfirmed ). Ghidra 's decompiler does not model every instruction; an unaff_* or CONCAT expression is a sign to read the disassembly. Float comparisons that look odd ( ucomiss plus parity checks) encode NaN handling that the replacement has to keep. Imports and system calls Library calls are linked by NID (a hash of the symbol name), not by name. Ghidra shows stubs. Names come from public NID databases, not from the binary. Unconfirmed for this target's import layout. System calls go through the libkernel wrappers; rax holds the syscall number. Hooks The hook is a 14-byte absolute jump ( jmp [rip+0] plus the target) written over the start of the original function. Shorter functions cannot be hooked that way. Nothing may jump into the first 14 bytes of a hooked function from elsewhere: check the references to the function's start region in Ghidra before hooking. A replacement calls library functions through the game's own thunks (declared with RT_ORIGINAL ), not through host libraries, so whatever answers the original's calls (the verification harness 's stubs, or the runtime ) answers the replacement's the same way. Verification traps A replacement that returns the same value can still differ in memory writes. Write order does not matter but final bytes do: verify.py compares the final byte map. Uninitialized padding in structs is copied by the original. Replacement code that zeroes padding fails verify.py on memory writes; decide per case and record it in the function's note. Ghidra hides code after the engine's fatal error call Ghidra marks the engine's fatal error function ( 0x024b55b0 , "file, line, message") as non-returning, so the bytes after a call to it are not disassembled unless something jumps there. The game's code does continue there (a jump to the return, or to another report), which matters when a replacement is tested with that function stubbed. If a draft's disassembly has a gap after such a call, disassemble the bytes directly (objdump on the ELF ) before writing the replacement. Example: kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ) returns -3 after the EINVAL report. A community patch edit that calls into the middle of another function Uncap FPS++ replaces vmovss xmm4, [0x04d29e74] (1/30 s) at 0x02715d71 , in 0x02713870 , with call 0x027166f7 and three nop s. In v1.09, 0x027166f7 is in the middle of a static initialiser ( 0x02716680 , 231 bytes), just before an engine fatal-error call and stores to globals; no line of any patch in the file writes code there. Run that way, the block would call the fatal error, overwrite the initialiser's globals and return through an epilogue whose pushes never happened. The patched block is a cold path placed after the function's return, so it may simply never run. There is nothing faithful to replicate: a replacement keeps the stock 1/30 s there, and the option check for Uncap FPS++ cannot cover that block.
docs.title: Ghidra & PS4 Quirks

docs.text: The ELF has no section headers (confirmed). The Orbis loader ( GhidraOrbis ) synthesizes blocks from the program headers: the executable PT_LOAD becomes .text , and its own heuristic splits .rodata , .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr off the end of it. The progress denominator is the functions Ghidra finds in that .text block, so it depends on the loader and the analysis. progress.py ties its numbers to the hash of the committed export, and the export prints how many functions fell outside .text . .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr are marked executable by the loader ; they are data. e_type is 0xfe10 (confirmed), not ET_EXEC or ET_DYN . The first PT_LOAD has p_vaddr 0, so the file does not say where the game lives; the convention below does. Ghidra 's default for this file type is unconfirmed : always set the image base explicitly on import and check it (the export script refuses any other base). Program headers include Sony types ( PT_SCE_* , PT_SCE_DYNLIBDATA and friends) that Ghidra does not understand. The PT_INTERP is /libexec/ld-elf.so.1 (confirmed). Dynamic linking data is in a Sony-specific segment, so Ghidra will not resolve imports by itself. SelfUtil-Patched removes the repeated data before the first segment (at 0x4000) and patches the version segment. Another SelfUtil build can produce a different file with different hashes: always check target.sha256 .
docs.title: The converted executable

docs.text: All addresses in this repository are PS4 virtual addresses: the ELF p_vaddr plus 0x400000 , with Ghidra 's image base set to 0x400000 . Community patch files use the same address convention. Three conventions exist, one constant apart. V is the ELF p_vaddr . Convention Address Where it appears ELF virtual address V ELF program headers and file layout PS4 virtual address V + 0x400000 ours , Ghidra , community patch files To convert an address to the ELF virtual address, subtract 0x400000 . tools/validate_functions.py rejects any address below 0x00400000 , which catches a base-0 import by mistake. Checked against the target image (read-only): - The community "Performance Patch" address 0x0261B108 minus 0x400000 holds c7 45 b4 06 00 00 00 ( mov dword [rbp-0x4c], 6 ), which the patch changes to 9. Tool-independent identity: the loaded image (loadable segments copied to their p_vaddr , SHA-256) of this target is 071df19c8880086d97182dbc057bc8cb37badaca57d9112683836b24a0444c0a . It is the same whichever SelfUtil build produced the ELF .
docs.title: Address conventions

docs.text: Ghidra 12 headless has no Jython: a .py script fails with " Ghidra was not started with PyGhidra". Our scripts are Java GhidraScripts. support/analyzeHeadless hardcodes MAXMEM=2G . That is too small for this binary; raise it in that file (setup in docs/GHIDRA.md). The Orbis loader replaces an image base of 0 by 0x1000000 by default. Pass -loader-imageBase 0x400000 ( -loader-baseAddr is ignored by this loader ). -loader "Orbis ELF" is rejected by headless as an invalid loader name; leave -loader out, the Orbis loader is picked automatically for this file.
docs.title: Ghidra itself

docs.text: Orbis uses the System V AMD64 ABI: integer arguments in rdi rsi rdx rcx r8 r9 , floats in xmm0-xmm7 , return in rax:rdx / xmm0:xmm1 , callee-saved rbx rbp r12-r15 . Variadic callers set al to the number of vector registers. Leaf functions use the 128-byte red zone below rsp . Ghidra 's stack analysis can read that as unused or mis-size the frame. Optimized code splits and merges functions (tail calls, shared epilogues, cold paths in the same range). A "function" boundary in Ghidra may be wrong. Check the call sites before you claim a size. Parameters Ghidra types as undefined8 are often pointers or floats in another register class. Read the call sites, not the decompiler's signature. Ghidra can pick a wrong calling convention for functions that pass a struct or this in an unusual register. Fix the signature before trusting the output.
docs.title: Calling convention

docs.text: The CPU is an AMD Jaguar: SSE up to 4.2, AVX and F16C, BMI1. No AVX2, BMI2 or FMA3 ( unconfirmed ). Ghidra 's decompiler does not model every instruction; an unaff_* or CONCAT expression is a sign to read the disassembly. Float comparisons that look odd ( ucomiss plus parity checks) encode NaN handling that the replacement has to keep.
docs.title: CPU

docs.text: Library calls are linked by NID (a hash of the symbol name), not by name. Ghidra shows stubs. Names come from public NID databases, not from the binary. Unconfirmed for this target's import layout. System calls go through the libkernel wrappers; rax holds the syscall number.
docs.title: Imports and system calls

docs.text: The hook is a 14-byte absolute jump ( jmp [rip+0] plus the target) written over the start of the original function. Shorter functions cannot be hooked that way. Nothing may jump into the first 14 bytes of a hooked function from elsewhere: check the references to the function's start region in Ghidra before hooking. A replacement calls library functions through the game's own thunks (declared with RT_ORIGINAL ), not through host libraries, so whatever answers the original's calls (the verification harness 's stubs, or the runtime ) answers the replacement's the same way.
docs.title: Hooks

docs.text: A replacement that returns the same value can still differ in memory writes. Write order does not matter but final bytes do: verify.py compares the final byte map. Uninitialized padding in structs is copied by the original. Replacement code that zeroes padding fails verify.py on memory writes; decide per case and record it in the function's note.

docs.text: Glossary: PS4 and port terms A running glossary for terms used across the devlog and the system pages. Hover any of them on another page for a short definition. Functional decompilation Rewriting the game's code as readable source that behaves exactly like the original, checked by running both on the same inputs. A matching decompilation goes further and requires the rebuilt bytes to be identical; this project does not, because the goal is a native port, not the original binary. What it does require is that every replaced function does the same thing: the same return value, the same memory written, the same calls made. Source port The game rebuilt from source to run natively somewhere else, here on a PC. It is where Paleblood is headed, not what it is today: the game does not run on Paleblood until its own runtime is far enough along. Replaced, edge-verified and verified A function is replaced once a hook sends every call to our C++ and the game library builds. It is edge-verified once the harness found no difference from the original on every generated edge case , but nobody has recorded it in the game yet: some code only runs in places a recording can't reach without the right save, such as the Chalice Dungeons. It is verified once the harness also found no difference on every case recorded in the game, deliberately wrong versions of it failed, and the game ran with it in place. An edge-verified function becomes verified on its own: tools/promote.py re-checks it when recordings for it appear, and promotes it only if all of them pass. Boot milestone and import coverage The runtime track measures how far the game's executable gets on Paleblood's own runtime . Import coverage is the share of the system functions the executable imports that the runtime implements. A boot milestone is the first call to a family of system functions, in the runtime roadmap's order: entry, threads, files, input, audio, video out, GPU, first flip. A boot stops at the first import that isn't implemented yet, and the boot harness names it. Hook A 14-byte jump written over the first bytes of an original function, pointing at the replacement. Every caller still calls the original address and lands in the replacement. A function shorter than the jump cannot be hooked this way. The hook table is installed by the runtime once it runs the game; the verification harness calls replacements directly. Harness, captures and edge cases The harness runs the original function from your own dump and its replacement, natively, outside the game, on the same inputs. Captures are inputs recorded while the game ran (the existing library was recorded on the old borrowed runtime ; Paleblood's own recorder now has a stable, self-identifying output format, but still needs production call sites); edge cases are generated for situations a short run does not reach. Mutation test Deliberately wrong versions of a replacement go through verification too: each must fail. If one passes, the cases cannot see that difference, and they are fixed before anything is called verified . PS4 , Orbis The PlayStation 4 runs an AMD x86-64 CPU (Jaguar) and Orbis OS, derived from FreeBSD. Because the CPU is x86-64 like a PC's, the game's code can run directly on a PC once something provides the operating system around it. SELF , ELF , PRX , eboot An ELF is the standard executable format of Linux and FreeBSD. The PS4 wraps executables in a SELF (signed ELF ); ours are fake-signed and unencrypted, so turning them back into ELFs only unwraps them. The main executable is eboot.bin ; PRX files are the PS4 's shared libraries. NID PS4 programs link to library functions by NID : a hash of the function's name. GhidraOrbis carries a database that turns NIDs back into names, so sceKernelUsleep shows up instead of a hash. Thunk A tiny piece of code that only forwards a call. The game calls each PS4 library function through a thunk ; our replacements call the same thunks , so whatever answers the original's calls (the harness 's scripted stubs, or the runtime ) answers the replacement's the same way. Runtime and loader The runtime is what the game's code runs on: Paleblood's own loader , which maps the executable and the game's own C library and file system modules and binds every system import, and its own versions of the PS4 system libraries, written clean-room. The project-owned runtime does not yet run the full game; see Runtime . GNM , PM4 , GCN GNM is the PS4 's low-level graphics API; the game builds PM4 command packets for its AMD GCN graphics chip. Paleblood does not plan to emulate that chip: the graphics are to be rebuilt at the level of the game's own graphics layer, on Vulkan. FDE A Frame Description Entry: one function's unwind record in the executable's .eh_frame . Counting them gave an independent check on how many functions Ghidra found. vblank and flip The screen refreshes at a fixed rate; the gap between two refreshes is the vertical blank. A flip shows a finished frame at a vblank . The frame limiter can flip every vblank (60 frames a second on a 60 Hz screen) or every other one (30).

docs.text: How the Frame Limiter Works The first system of Bloodborne replaced in C++ is the one that decides how long each frame lasts. This page walks through it as the original does it, and as the replacement now does it, exactly the same way. next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work Where it sits Every frame, frame_timing_frame_step asks the window whether the game is still running, and on the very first frame creates the game's frame-pacing object, the SprjFlipper . Its constructor, frame_timing_flipper_init , reads one value from the game's configuration: Game.FlipMode . Then the frame step calls the flipper's limiter, frame_timing_pace_frame , and only after it returns lets the game do its frame of work. So the limiter runs at the start of every frame, and its job is to make sure the previous frame took long enough. Choosing the pace The flip mode picks one of five settings. Each sets two things in the flipper: the frame interval (a float, in seconds) and the sync interval (how many vblanks a flip waits for). Mode Frame interval Sync interval 0, 1 1/30 s 2 2 1/60 s 1 3, 4 1/30 s 1 A pending mode can replace the current one at the start of a frame; a few flags reset the pacing state, for example after a load. Waiting out the frame The limiter reads the time with gettimeofday , works out how much of the frame's budget is left, and waits. The game carries two ways of waiting: one that sleeps in chunks and spins the last few milliseconds, and one that only spins, reading the clock again and again until the time is up. A switch compiled into this build always picks the spinning one, which is why a quick frame can read the clock hundreds of thousands of times. It is precise, and it keeps one CPU core busy. The budget is not always the full interval. The flipper keeps the last 32 frame times in a ring, marking the frames that ran late; if recent frames ran over, the next budget is shortened to catch up, but never below a third of the interval. Afterwards The limiter records the frame's time in the ring, decides whether this frame counts as late (and if so drops the sync interval to 0 so the next flip does not wait for a vblank ), and keeps a 16-frame history from which it computes the frame rate the game reports. If a flag asks for it, it also tells another object that the game now targets 60 frames a second. The replacement The C++ version follows the original instruction by instruction, including how it converts between integers and floating point and how each comparison treats a value that is not a number. It was compared with the original on every frame recorded in two game runs, including frames that spin on the clock for hundreds of thousands of reads, and on hand-written cases for every mode and flag; four deliberately wrong versions all failed. It also carries the port's first setting, BB_TARGET_FPS : unset, nothing changes; 30 , 60 and uncapped do what the community frame-rate patches do here (a fixed interval of 1/30, 1/60 or 1/240 s, no overrides), and the frame step passes the game the real frame time, as those patches do. Each part is checked against the patch itself. See the frame timing page .

docs.text: Runtime system-call notes This page records the public API contracts and the evidence currently available for calls in runtime issue #34 , with a separate network byte-order slice from issue #41 . A platform manual describes that platform; it does not prove every detail of the PS4 implementation. The notes below separate documented behavior from what remains unknown for the target. What the game evidence shows The executable imports getpagesize and gettimeofday from libScePosix . The game's bundled libc.elf imports clock_gettime , getpagesize , getpid , and gettimeofday from libkernel . These import rows establish required names, not every call argument or the behavior of the PS4 implementation. The frame limiter calls gettimeofday with a null timezone argument. A separate verified game helper calls sceKernelClockGettime with clock ID 4 , identified as CLOCK_MONOTONIC . This confirms that ID for the SCE entry point. It does not establish which IDs the game passes to the imported clock_gettime wrapper, or whether 4 is accepted there. Interfaces and behavior Call Arguments and representation Publicly documented result and errors Still unknown for the PS4 target getpagesize(void) No arguments; returns the system page size in bytes. The number is platform-specific. Linux and FreeBSD document the byte count. getpagesize is not in current POSIX; portable code uses sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) . The manuals do not define a general error return. The target's page-size value and behavior under unusual configurations. Never substitute the build host's page size without evidence. getpid(void) No arguments; returns a pid_t for the calling process. POSIX specifies success and no error return. Linux PID namespaces scope process IDs; process-ID scope and lifetime are platform-specific. The guest-visible ID and its scope. The host PID is not automatically the correct guest result. clock_gettime(clock_id, tp) clock_id selects a clock. tp points to a struct timespec ; POSIX represents it as seconds ( tv_sec ) and nanoseconds ( tv_nsec ), normalized so tv_nsec is from 0 through 999,999,999. POSIX returns 0 on success and -1 with errno on failure; an unsupported clock ID is EINVAL . Linux and BSD manuals document pointer errors, but exact error mapping is platform-specific. The target structure layout, IDs accepted by the imported wrapper, and its pointer/error behavior. ID 4 is confirmed only for sceKernelClockGettime . gettimeofday(tv, tz) tv points to a struct timeval : seconds since the Epoch and microseconds ( tv_usec from 0 through 999,999). The game passes null for tz . This is wall time and may jump; it is not a monotonic elapsed-time clock. Older POSIX specified 0 on success but left errors undefined. Linux reports -1 / EFAULT for inaccessible pointers and ignores tz . POSIX.1-2024 removed the interface. The target structure layout, bad-pointer behavior, non-null timezone behavior, and error mapping. The known game call passes null for tz . The numeric clock IDs in POSIX are implementation-defined. Linux also has IDs such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME ; FreeBSD has its own clock set, including CLOCK_UPTIME variants. Those names and numbers are not evidence for PS4 behavior. No inspected source confirms that the game's imported clock_gettime receives CLOCK_REALTIME , CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW , CLOCK_BOOTTIME , or any ID besides the separate SCE call's value 4. Network byte-order conversions Paleblood imports four integer conversion calls from libSceNet in eboot : sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs . Their public SCE declarations use unsigned 32-bit and 16-bit integer arguments and results. The documented byte-order contract converts between host order and big-endian network order; the reverse direction uses the same operation. For the project's AMD64 guest ABI, this is byte reversal. The four calls are pure value conversions and do not require socket or online state. The declaration reference below is PSP2SDK's public net.h API surface; it supplies the SCE function names and integer widths, not a PS4 runtime trace. The FreeBSD manual documents the standard host/network conversion contract. This evidence supports only these four conversions. It does not establish behavior for libSceNet sockets, name resolution, epoll, or offline-state queries. Those imports remain unimplemented until their own evidence is available. Implementation and tests Implement only behavior supported by public documentation, independent reverse engineering, or observed behavior. Keep unresolved target behavior visible; do not fabricate a return value to make tools/boot.py advance. Add cases to the RT_SYSLIB unit test for each established behavior and error path. Runtime-only contributions do not need a game dump, captures , or function-level verify.py results; CI builds and runs the runtime and syslib tests. References POSIX clock_gettime , POSIX clock definitions , and POSIX getpid Older POSIX gettimeofday specification FreeBSD getpagesize(3) , clock_gettime(2) , and gettimeofday(2) Linux getpagesize(2) , getpid(2) , clock_gettime(2) , and gettimeofday(2) PSP2SDK network API declarations for the four SCE byte-order functions FreeBSD htonl(3) / htons(3) / ntohl(3) / ntohs(3)

ID 4 is confirmed only for sceKernelClockGettime . gettimeofday(tv, tz) tv points to a struct timeval : seconds since the Epoch and microseconds ( tv_usec from 0 through 999,999). The game passes null for tz . This is wall time and may jump; it is not a monotonic elapsed-time clock. Older POSIX specified 0 on success but left errors undefined. Linux reports -1 / EFAULT for inaccessible pointers and ignores tz . POSIX.1-2024 removed the interface. The target structure layout, bad-pointer behavior, non-null timezone behavior, and error mapping. The known game call passes null for tz . The numeric clock IDs in POSIX are implementation-defined. Linux also has IDs such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME ; FreeBSD has its own clock set, including CLOCK_UPTIME variants. Those names and numbers are not evidence for PS4 behavior. No inspected source confirms that the game's imported clock_gettime receives CLOCK_REALTIME , CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW , CLOCK_BOOTTIME , or any ID besides the separate SCE call's value 4.

docs.text: Paleblood imports four integer conversion calls from libSceNet in eboot : sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs . Their public SCE declarations use unsigned 32-bit and 16-bit integer arguments and results. The documented byte-order contract converts between host order and big-endian network order; the reverse direction uses the same operation. For the project's AMD64 guest ABI, this is byte reversal. The four calls are pure value conversions and do not require socket or online state. The declaration reference below is PSP2SDK's public net.h API surface; it supplies the SCE function names and integer widths, not a PS4 runtime trace. The FreeBSD manual documents the standard host/network conversion contract. This evidence supports only these four conversions. It does not establish behavior for libSceNet sockets, name resolution, epoll, or offline-state queries. Those imports remain unimplemented until their own evidence is available.

docs.text: Runtime Paleblood is building a runtime of its own. A runtime is the software that loads a program and provides the system services it expects. The project has an ELF loader and boot harness that can load the game's executable and bundled system modules, bind imports, and run the entry point until it reaches a call the current runtime does not implement. That is different from running the full game. Full native game runs still use a third-party host scaffold for the broader execution environment, system-library coverage, and Vulkan rendering. Paleblood supplies a project-owned hook plug-in and host interface, but the project-owned runtime has not replaced that host or passed equivalent full-run checks. What works in Paleblood's runtime ELF loading and boot diagnostics. runtime/loader.c maps the executable and bundled modules, applies relocations, and binds known imports. runtime/boot.c and tools/boot.py run the entry point and record how far it gets. Selected system calls. The runtime supplies a small set of kernel/thread calls and four libSceNet byte-order conversions: sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs . These convert 16-bit and 32-bit integer byte order; they do not implement sockets or online services. See runtime system-call notes and issue #41 for the live group status. Function replacements and hooks . The project's plug-in receives the guest image and a hook -install callback, then registers its function replacements. The small host-interface test uses a synthetic host to check this contract; it does not test the third-party host or run the game. Runtime System imports provided 238 of 686 (34.69%): 219 by the game's own modules, 19 by the runtime ; 448 remaining Furthest boot milestone loaded (0 of 8) Boot stops at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (libkernel, called by libc.elf) Last recorded run: 2026-10-07. This is saved evidence, not a live measurement. Generated by tools/sync_progress.py from the code repo. Do not edit. The table above is generated from the saved Paleblood boot record. Its date identifies the last recorded run; changing runtime code does not refresh the result by itself. Capture and replay Paleblood has a local capture writer and replay verifier. Saved cases carry function and run identifiers, use stable buffer ordering, and replay checks reject a case for a different function or address. The version-1 production hook interface does not observe function returns or describe pointer buffers, and current replacements do not call the recorder. A separate test adapter proves that explicitly described synthetic inputs can be serialized and replayed. This checks the case format and verifier path only. It does not capture real game calls, prove a replacement against a real recording, or supply production run inputs. tools/promote.py consumes existing recorded cases and generated edge cases ; it does not create captures . Boot history and the current blocker PR #51 extended new symbols/boot_history.csv rows with the run outcome, execution phase, unresolved-import return site, and guest-fault location, signal, and address. A changed failure location is recorded even when import counts and the blocking symbol stay the same. Existing rows remain readable. This improved diagnostics; it did not run the game or change the saved boot result. The issue #34 runtime work for kernel, threads, and memory is still claimed in its public issue , and no corresponding runtime change has merged. The next maintainer boot run is gated on that relevant change merging. It should then compare the new history fields against the saved baseline instead of inferring progress from import counts alone. Kernel, threads, and memory: the present boot blocker. Issue #34 is contributor-claimed; preserve that ownership and run the harness after the relevant change merges. Capture integration: add a return-aware, ABI-described observation boundary before connecting recordings to production hooks . Synthetic tests are not a substitute for real captures . Files, input, audio, and video output: implement and measure each milestone as the boot harness reaches it. GNM and shaders: rebuild the game's graphics layer at its engine interface, then prove the first rendered frame. System-library work is tracked separately from boot milestones. The four byte-order calls above are the only currently implemented functions in the network issue group; sockets, resolvers, epoll, and offline-state behavior remain unresolved. Paleblood's own pbboot harness builds and tests without that submodule, but it does not yet provide equivalent full-game loading, services, rendering, or route checks. The scaffold and its required attribution stay in the code repository until a project-owned replacement passes the same native game-run checks.

docs.text: 6 October 2026: from an empty repository to the frame loop The first day: the target was prepared, the repositories and tooling were set up, and the first Ghidra export and verified frame-loop replacements were completed, from the clock up to the function that runs every frame. The target Both packages extracted without keys and merged. The update's param.sfo reports the 1.09 app version. All eight executables (the eboot and seven PRX modules) were fake-signed SELFs with no encrypted segments, and converting them to ELF only unwrapped them. Hashes are on the Target page. Repositories and tooling progress.py derives every number from symbols/ in the code repository. verify.py runs the original code and a replacement side by side, outside the game, on the same inputs, and compares everything they do (more on that below). The pre-commit hooks refuse game data, local notes and stale progress numbers. The converted eboot has no section headers, so there is no .text to measure. The progress denominator is the set of functions Ghidra finds in executable blocks, tied to the hash of the committed export. The first Ghidra export Ghidra 12.0.3 with the GhidraOrbis loader imported the eboot and finished full auto-analysis in about 26 minutes. It found 157,757 functions in .text , 42,487,347 bytes, not counting 9,302 thunks . All 671 imports resolved to names through the NID database. The loader decides where .text ends with a heuristic, and on a small module it put almost all the code into .rodata , where nothing gets analyzed. So the export needed a check that does not depend on Ghidra at all: the unwind table. It lists 162,959 functions. 155,000 of them are functions in the export, and the other 7,959 are all thunks , which the export skips on purpose. Ghidra also found 2,757 functions that have no unwind entry. The gap is fully accounted for. That is the size of the job: about 158 thousand functions and 42 MB of code. The first function: a millisecond clock 0x0111a7f0 turned out to be a monotonic millisecond clock: it asks the system for CLOCK_MONOTONIC , keeps the seconds of its first call in a shared state object, and returns the milliseconds since then. The C++ replacement does the same, down to the 32-bit arithmetic that wraps. To check the checker, deliberately broken versions of each replacement are run through verify.py ; each must fail. Then the game runs with the hook installed, the replacement records its real inputs as it goes, and those recordings are compared too: over 30,000 calls in 90 seconds here, and the game reached the title menu exactly as it does without the hook . Two bugs were caught before anything was marked verified : the recording code dropped half of each clock value, and the tester counted cases from two runs as one when they shared names. With the monitors off, the desktop throttles a game window to one frame a second. A virtual display ( Xvfb ) fixes that for test runs, at about 15 frames a second on the title screen. Finding the frame limiter The plan was to walk outward from the millisecond clock to the frame limiter. But the clock and its two neighbours have 52 callers, all in one stretch of the executable and none touched by any frame-rate patch: a separate subsystem, not the frame loop. The frame-rate patches by Kyo (and Lance McDonald for the uncapped one) were written by people who already found the limiter. Mapping every patched address to its function, then keeping the functions that both read the clock and sleep, left one that every frame-rate patch edits: 0x02434770 , now frame_timing_pace_frame . The frame limiter article explains how it works. The limiter, replaced , and the first option The replacement follows the original instruction by instruction, down to how it converts between integers and floating point and how each comparison treats NaN. Twenty-six hand-written cases cover every mode; four deliberately wrong versions all fail, after two of them first got through and showed the cases had blind spots. In-game recordings, with the community patches off so the original is the real one, all match. The spinning wait broke the first recording: frames with more than 20,000 clock reads were dropped, which removed exactly the frames that spin. Runs of clock reads are now stored as one series. BB_TARGET_FPS set to 30 , 60 or uncapped changes the limiter in code, the way the community patches change it with byte edits. Unset, nothing changes. It covers only the limiter: the patches also fix many places where the game assumes 30 frames a second, and those still need the patch until they are replaced too. BB_LIMITER_WAIT=sleep makes the limiter sleep instead of spinning while it waits. Both wait for a measurement on a real screen. The frame step and the flipper frame_timing_frame_step is the function the main loop calls once per frame. It asks the window object whether the game is still running, creates the frame-pacing object on the first frame, runs the limiter, runs the game's task update, and asks two more objects whether the player has asked to quit. Four of those questions are virtual calls, so it was the first function whose inputs are objects: the recordings now describe each object as a small stand-in whose table slot points at the real function the game called. It matched on every recorded frame. frame_timing_flipper_init builds the frame-pacing object. It reads the config value Game.FlipMode twice through the game's own string class; the shipped config leaves it unset, which is why the game runs the 30 FPS mode. Verified on the recorded call and nine edge cases . The microsecond time helper the frame-rate patches edit is replaced too, but the game never calls it before the title menu, so it waits for a run that gets further. The frame-rate option, corrected A function nothing calls turned out to be a code cave: the time helper the frame-rate patches edit is never called in the stock game, and the patches overwrite it with their own code. That led to a closer look at what the patches do to the functions we did replace, by disassembling each with and without the patch. They do more than the limiter: they also make the frame step hand the game the measured frame time instead of a fixed 1/30 s. Our hooked frame step had switched that off, so the first version of BB_TARGET_FPS=60 would have run the game logic twice as fast. The test harness can now apply a patch to the original code, so each part of the option is checked against the patch itself: all edge cases , every deliberately wrong version caught, and frames recorded at 60 FPS in the game match. A real-screen measurement waits for the display plug. Counting calls, and three more functions Of the 59 functions the frame-rate patches touch outside frame timing, 12 turned out to be dead code and 47 live. To find which of the live ones the game actually runs, the runtime can now count calls to original functions without replacing them: a short jump at each entry to a counter that then runs the original. One gameplay run in Iosefka's Clinic showed 13 of them running, several every frame. Nine of the others are small state methods that advance an owner by a fixed 1/30 s step; they are built next to the game's Chalice Dungeon singleton and do not run in the clinic. They are replaced and checked against the 60 FPS patch, and wait for a save that reaches the Chalice Dungeons. A per-frame task that hands the frame time to its parts is replaced and verified , including what the uncapped patch does to it through a code cave. And the engine's condition variable wait is the first function of a new system, the engine's kernel layer: the patches put a return over its timed wait that would crash if it ran, and every wait the game made was untimed. One trap on the way: Ghidra treats the engine's fatal error as a call that never returns, so it hides the instructions right after it. The game's code does continue there, and a replacement written from the listing alone got one path wrong until the bytes were read directly. Workflow The work no longer waits on the maintainer between steps: a target queue, a standing procedure, a smoke test of the whole pipeline at the start of each session, a lock that keeps two projects off the GPU at the same time, and one game run records inputs for every replaced function at once. Checking the limiter's recordings used to keep a core busy for four minutes; with a native answer for the clock reads, the executable loaded once and low priority, it takes under one. Replacements may start from a draft of the decompiler's output, kept on the maintainer's machine and never committed. What is committed is the renamed, readable, verified version. This wiki The site theme and the one-post-per-day devlog were established alongside the project's documentation. Next The live functions the 60 FPS patches edit, starting with the frame-time descriptor family. The other places the frame-rate patches edit.

It asks the window object whether the game is still running, creates the frame-pacing object on the first frame, runs the limiter, runs the game's task update, and asks two more objects whether the player has asked to quit. Four of those questions are virtual calls, so it was the first function whose inputs are objects: the recordings now describe each object as a small stand-in whose table slot points at the real function the game called. It matched on every recorded frame. frame_timing_flipper_init builds the frame-pacing object. It reads the config value Game.FlipMode twice through the game's own string class; the shipped config leaves it unset, which is why the game runs the 30 FPS mode. Verified on the recorded call and nine edge cases . The microsecond time helper the frame-rate patches edit is replaced too, but the game never calls it before the title menu, so it waits for a run that gets further.
docs.title: The frame step and the flipper

docs.text: A function nothing calls turned out to be a code cave: the time helper the frame-rate patches edit is never called in the stock game, and the patches overwrite it with their own code. That led to a closer look at what the patches do to the functions we did replace, by disassembling each with and without the patch. They do more than the limiter: they also make the frame step hand the game the measured frame time instead of a fixed 1/30 s. Our hooked frame step had switched that off, so the first version of BB_TARGET_FPS=60 would have run the game logic twice as fast. The test harness can now apply a patch to the original code, so each part of the option is checked against the patch itself: all edge cases , every deliberately wrong version caught, and frames recorded at 60 FPS in the game match. A real-screen measurement waits for the display plug.
docs.title: The frame-rate option, corrected

docs.text: Of the 59 functions the frame-rate patches touch outside frame timing, 12 turned out to be dead code and 47 live. To find which of the live ones the game actually runs, the runtime can now count calls to original functions without replacing them: a short jump at each entry to a counter that then runs the original. One gameplay run in Iosefka's Clinic showed 13 of them running, several every frame. Nine of the others are small state methods that advance an owner by a fixed 1/30 s step; they are built next to the game's Chalice Dungeon singleton and do not run in the clinic. They are replaced and checked against the 60 FPS patch, and wait for a save that reaches the Chalice Dungeons. A per-frame task that hands the frame time to its parts is replaced and verified , including what the uncapped patch does to it through a code cave. And the engine's condition variable wait is the first function of a new system, the engine's kernel layer: the patches put a return over its timed wait that would crash if it ran, and every wait the game made was untimed. One trap on the way: Ghidra treats the engine's fatal error as a call that never returns, so it hides the instructions right after it. The game's code does continue there, and a replacement written from the listing alone got one path wrong until the bytes were read directly.
docs.title: Counting calls, and three more functions

docs.text: The work no longer waits on the maintainer between steps: a target queue, a standing procedure, a smoke test of the whole pipeline at the start of each session, a lock that keeps two projects off the GPU at the same time, and one game run records inputs for every replaced function at once. Checking the limiter's recordings used to keep a core busy for four minutes; with a native answer for the clock reads, the executable loaded once and low priority, it takes under one. Replacements may start from a draft of the decompiler's output, kept on the maintainer's machine and never committed. What is committed is the renamed, readable, verified version.

docs.text: 7 October 2026: a new direction, our own runtime Paleblood opened its code to contributors and began building a clean-room runtime of its own. This entry combines the day's runtime work and decompilation progress. Runtime and boot progress Earlier that day, the former runtime ran the game at 60 FPS through Iosefka's Clinic. The project then began removing that borrowed runtime and its graphics dependency. Paleblood's new loader maps the executable byte for byte and its verification harness reproduced the earlier function results. At this point the new runtime did not run the game; its system-library work stopped at an unimplemented import. The roadmap still included threads and memory, files, input, audio, video out, and graphics. Decompilation and verified functions The frame-loop work included the pad manager's step, reference-counted render updates, present/ vblank handling, YEBIS sample parameters, six task-manager functions, a physics constructor, the Havok AI manager, and a character update. Existing cases cover per-frame work and 19 physics constructions. The AI manager's branches and idle paths use explicit test fixtures. Tests caught floating-point edge cases , stack arguments, thread-local state, shared patch data, and object memory that the harness needed to describe. Tooling and automation The verification harness learned to pass and return floating-point values, model stack arguments and thread-local state, apply the frame-rate patch to the original, and count calls without replacing functions. Deliberately incorrect replacements were used to check that the cases caught known mistakes. The project also introduced a readable-code review gate and a contributor route based on claimed work and pull-request evidence. Documentation and website changes The public Paleblood repository opened with contribution guidance and protected pull requests. The runtime roadmap and clean-room boundary were documented alongside the new loader . Tests and validation The verification harness ran existing recorded and edge cases , and deliberately wrong versions exposed several test gaps. The new loader reproduced the same verification results. These checks validated function behavior; they did not demonstrate full game execution on the project-owned runtime . Blockers and next steps At the time, the new runtime still needed its system imports and execution layers before it could boot the game. The decompilation continued independently, with every replacement requiring recorded inputs where available, edge cases , readable code, and matching verification evidence.

docs.text: 9 October 2026: a path for runtime contributors Runtime-only contributors can implement a documented syscall without access to a game dump or recorded captures . This day's work prepared the issue #34 contribution route and clarified what the current boot evidence does and does not establish. Runtime and boot progress The runtime still stopped at its first unresolved system call. The maintainer's boot check runs locally after a runtime pull request merges; a contributor does not need proprietary files or captures to implement and test a runtime -only change. Decompilation and verified functions No function replacement or verification status changed in this milestone. The frame limiter's clock calls pass a null timezone to gettimeofday ; a separate sceKernelClockGettime call uses clock ID 4 , but the IDs passed to the imported clock_gettime are still unknown. Those gaps remain open instead of being filled with assumed return values. Tooling and automation The issue #34 workflow uses a claim-and-branch process, small related changes, and a concise evidence report. Paleblood PR #44 , merged at ef1989ec3388c26cddd20b13742ba93d09cc147e , prepared the contributor checks. Runtime-only pull requests use the compiler matrix, system-library tests, and policy checks. Decompilation and mixed changes retain the full session report and verification gates. Shared Git hooks dispatch through the active worktree, so linked worktrees use their own installed checks. Daily posting now updates the existing local-date entry through stable milestone keys, ordered sections, and concurrent-safe atomic writes. The gated publisher also keeps the pinned Paleblood source revision separate from the public-site remote. Seven deterministic tests pass, including concurrent updates and repeat MkDocs output. These are documentation and workflow improvements; game execution did not advance. Paleblood PR #51 , merged at fe3661f , keeps boot outcome, phase, unresolved-import return site, and guest fault location in history, including when only the failure site changes. GCC and Clang builds and CTest passed 11/11 each; 93 Python tests passed. This improves diagnostics only; no game run or boot advancement occurred. Documentation and website changes The syscall notes distinguish public contracts for getpagesize , getpid , clock_gettime , and gettimeofday from target-specific behavior not yet established. The loading map records the bundled Fios module while leaving archive access, PlayGo flow, and target-specific error paths as open questions. Progress was synchronized from merged Paleblood sources. Paleblood PR #52 , merged at b7a5dc5 , clarifies that the current full game-run path still depends on the external scaffold pending equivalent project-owned run checks. This cleanup removes the legacy runtime study pages, test-run media, unverified wiki icon, and media-only build hook from Byrgenwerth, with focused checks against reintroduction in public source and generated output. GCC and Clang builds and CTest passed 11/11 each; the strict wiki build, 10 Python tests, hooks , and 88-file privacy scan passed. This improves documentation and publication safeguards; it does not advance game execution or decompilation. Tests and validation The issue #34 workflow added no replacement and no verification result. Runtime-only CI checks run without game data; pull-request CI validates the changed code and policy before the local post-merge boot check. The shared hook changes were exercised in linked worktrees. Blockers and next steps The first unresolved import and the target-specific behavior listed above still need evidence. The next runtime change should implement one documented call or a tightly related group, keep unknown behavior explicit, and include deterministic tests and its source basis. The current Paleblood source has nine edge-verified functions, but none has matching recorded calls in the available capture library; the read-only promotion dry run produced no candidate. Issue #34 still has a contributor claim and remains the earliest boot blocker. Issues #35–#40 are unclaimed, but their current issue scopes list imports without enough target-specific contracts for a safe implementation. The existing 0x0183ac60 worktree was left untouched, and 0x02713870 still has no matching recorded inputs. No runtime behavior or game execution advanced.

docs.text: 10 October 2026: recorded verification and runtime foundations This day improved capture reliability, verified one function from existing recorded calls, and added four deterministic network byte-order imports. The tooling work did not itself advance game execution. Runtime and boot progress Paleblood PR #50 , merged at 816ea964c2d5db49271ad3131cad4a24e3d0bcc5 , added sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs . These implement fixed-width host/network byte-order conversions; socket, resolver, epoll, and online behavior remain uncovered. The saved boot result still stopped at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (238/686 system imports provided), within contributor-owned issue #34. No boot run was made for this change. Decompilation and verified functions Paleblood PR #48 promoted frame_timing_pace_frame ( 0x02434770 ) using its existing evidence: 585/585 recorded calls and 26/26 edge cases . Its approved independent review remained in place. PR #49 refreshed generated public documentation from the merged verification result; it added no runtime behavior or new cases. The verified function count reached 21. Tooling and automation Paleblood PR #46 made capture output stable, recorded function/run provenance, refused unsafe paths and existing case files, and kept older schema-1 cases replayable. PR #47 added an isolated typed adapter proof with explicit signature and memory descriptors. Synthetic fixtures passed capture , serialization, replay, and verification; unsupported signatures and missing descriptors failed closed. Production replacements still do not call this adapter, so these tests produced no real game captures . Paleblood PR #53 , merged at fec0551 , makes runtime issue counts recognize registered RT_SYSLIB entries without waiting for a boot run. This corrected issue #41 : the four network byte-order helpers from PR #50 are now checked and the group reports 4/175 implemented. Focused parser/count tests and the 95-test Python suite passed; GCC/Clang builds and CTest passed 11/11 each. This improves progress tracking only; actual boot did not advance. Paleblood PR #54 , merged at 8abd5531f919047ee8d28bae7b16a0332f5fb764 , adds a synthetic fake-host test for the existing version-1 host API consumer. It checks version rejection, image handoff, guest-relative hook registration, named/address hook skips, probe ordering, and error propagation. GCC and Clang Release builds and CTest passed 12/12 each; policy, hooks , and required CI checks passed. This improves ABI regression coverage only: the legacy host remains active, no equivalent replacement exists, and boot execution did not advance. Documentation and website changes The frame-timing page and generated progress data were refreshed from merged Paleblood revision 816ea964c2d5db49271ad3131cad4a24e3d0bcc5 . The public site was published at 21e1d26 . The runtime notes keep the production observer and capture integration explicitly unfinished. Public source documents the synthetic limits alongside the results. The Runtime, Architecture, and CI Setup pages were audited and updated against Paleblood 8abd5531f919047ee8d28bae7b16a0332f5fb764 ; all 30 public wiki pages plus generated fragments, navigation, metadata, image references, and search output were reviewed. The former homepage artwork could not be restored because its creator and redistribution rights are unrecorded. Automatic synchronization remains inactive: no least-privilege App credentials exist, and the current sync path executes code from the public Paleblood checkout. A final output review also removed a Runtime-page link into the legacy scaffold README so retired integration names stay out of public routes and search content. The license and dependency findings remain in the private maintenance audit. This documentation work did not advance game execution. Tests and validation The capture changes passed GCC and Clang builds and all 11 CTest suites. The verification promotion used the 585 recorded calls plus 26 edge cases . The four network helpers passed registry tests with known byte patterns, zero, maximum-width values, and round trips; both compiler builds and all 11 CTest suites passed. Clean-room, policy, hook , and session audits also passed. Blockers and next steps No production capture integration or game execution advanced. 0x02713870 still has no matching recorded inputs and remains blocked. The earliest saved boot blocker remains the issue #34 affinity import; synthetic capture tests are not substitutes for matching recorded cases or production ABI evidence.

docs.text: AI Summary Enemy and NPC behaviour runs on Havok AI, driven by the game's SprjHkAiManager (singleton 0x059401a0 ). Once a frame, ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 ( 0x0222bc10 ): steps the Havok AI world with a fixed time step of 1/30 s; with its second flag (always set in the recordings), copies the frame object's matrices to the manager's view object and runs the AI debug display and drawing: a debug position (the camera's, or the player character's when the character manager exists), debug marks, a draw descriptor over every AI object in its groups (or over the whole manager), axis frames looked up in the manager's id map, and boxes, after resetting the render manager's debug state to its defaults. In the recordings from Iosefka's Clinic it resets its three groups, copies the matrices and draws each AI object; the debug display, axis frames, boxes and the manager-wide draw stay off. Scope still to map: the AI world step itself ( 0x021cdad0 ), the groups and objects, the behaviour of individual enemies. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x0222bc10 2693 ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 verified SprjHkAiManager per-frame update: steps the AI world by 1/30 s (the 60 FPS patches: 1/60), AI debug display and drawing Structs and globals Owner of the update: groups +0x2bc8 (count) and +0x2bd0 ( 0x20 bytes each: element count +0x8 , elements +0x10 , 0xb0 bytes each with an object count +0x58 and object list +0x60 ); debug display +0x2c18 / +0x2c20 ; flags +0x2c90 .. +0x2c98 ; box mode +0x2c68 ; axis-frame pairs (id, index) from +0x2cb8 , +0x2ec0 of them. SprjHkAiManager : AI world +0x10 (its id map at +0x10 ), view object +0x20 . Patch points The AI world's time step is 1/30 s; 60 FPS++ (and 90 FPS++ , 60FPS (no deltatime) ) make it 1/60 s. BB_TARGET_FPS=60 does the same; 30 FPS++ and Uncap FPS++ leave it. Open questions With Uncap FPS++ , the AI world still steps by 1/30 s each frame: does AI run faster at high frame rates?
